story.headline: M7.1 quake strikes southern Japan
story.summary: A magnitude-7.1 earthquake hit Kumamoto on Kyushu on 28 July, injuring at least 50 and prompting a tsunami advisory.
story.display_body: A magnitude-7.1 earthquake struck southwestern Japan on Tuesday 28 July, hitting Kumamoto prefecture on the island of Kyushu and injuring at least 50 people. The quake struck shortly before 16:30 local time at a shallow depth of about 10 km (roughly 6 miles), according to the US Geological Survey; the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) issued a tsunami advisory for waves of about one metre along the Ariake and Yatsushiro seas and urged people away from the coast. Several thousand homes lost power, rail services stopped, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi warned of strong shaking around Uki City and Makigawa Town. Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority reported no abnormalities at nearby nuclear plants. Kumamoto is the same prefecture devastated by a pair of major quakes in 2016.
story.why: Japan sits on the "Ring of Fire" and records roughly a fifth of the world's earthquakes, but a shallow M7.1 directly under a populated region is at the severe end and the tsunami and landslide risk will keep the response tense for days.

story.headline: Netanyahu and Zelenskyy meet Trump
story.summary: Netanyahu and Zelenskyy both met Trump in Washington on 28 July as a Senate Russia-sanctions vote loomed and the Iran and Ukraine wars converged.
story.display_body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy both descended on Washington on Tuesday 28 July to meet President Donald Trump, as a long-stalled Russia-sanctions bill neared a Senate vote and the wars in Iran and Ukraine visibly converged. Both leaders were in the US chiefly for the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a Trump ally and hawkish backer of both Israel and Ukraine who died on 11 July; Netanyahu was set to meet Trump with the US-Israel war on Iran topping the agenda, while Zelenskyy pressed for anti-ballistic-missile defences and help producing Patriot systems. The sanctions bill Graham championed would impose 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas - including China and India - and Trump has moved at the last minute to fold sanctions on Iran into the same package. The convergence is concrete: Ukraine attacked an Iranian tanker in the Caspian Sea on Saturday 25 July that it says was ferrying drones and components to Russia, Iran has vowed to retaliate, and Russia said more than 390 Ukrainian drones struck the Moscow region overnight. Trump has said talks with Iran are under way during the current pause in US strikes.
story.why: Two wars 2,500 km apart are being wired together through Washington's sanctions machinery and Iran's arms pipeline to Moscow - treat both leaders' framing as advocacy, since each is seeking Trump's backing.

story.headline: Seoul's Kospi plunges 10.8%
story.summary: South Korea's Kospi fell 10.8% on 28 July as Samsung and SK Hynix crashed on fears over China's chipmaking advances.
story.display_body: South Korea's Kospi stock index collapsed 10.8% on Tuesday 28 July, closing at 6,023.66 - its lowest since April - after a rout in chipmaking shares triggered trading circuit-breakers (automatic pauses meant to halt panic selling). Samsung Electronics sank 13.4% and SK Hynix 14.7%; together the two account for a large share of the Seoul market. The sell-off followed a report in the trade publication The Information that China has begun mass-producing homegrown deep-ultraviolet (DUV) lithography tools - the machines that print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers, and a capability Western and Korean firms had assumed China was years from matching - stoking fears that Chinese competition could erode the incumbents' lead. European markets opened slightly higher, suggesting the shock stayed largely regional for now.
story.why: Semiconductors are the backbone of South Korea's export economy, so a one-day drop this steep is a real macroeconomic event - and it signals investors are newly worried that China's chip progress could reset a market the West has dominated.

story.headline: Sudan's RSF chief vows to unleash fighters
story.summary: RSF leader Hemedti said on 27 July he will no longer restrain his fighters after the army retook the strategic El-Obeid-Khartoum road.
story.display_body: The head of Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Mohamed Hamdan Daglo ("Hemedti"), said on Monday 27 July he would "no longer hold back" his fighters, after his forces suffered a battlefield reverse near El-Obeid. Sudan's army said it had pushed the RSF westward and regained control of the strategic 400-km road linking El-Obeid, in North Kordofan, to the capital Khartoum, where the paramilitaries had massed for months in preparation for a large-scale assault; army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan toured a recaptured position alongside allied militia commanders. The RSF, whose forces stand accused of genocide in Sudan's two-year civil war, has been fighting the regular army since April 2023.
story.why: Hemedti's threat to unleash his fighters after losing ground points to a bloodier phase in a war that has already driven the world's largest displacement crisis, and the road's recapture eases pressure on the army's supply line to Khartoum.

story.headline: Chad moves to quit the ICC
story.summary: Chad announced it will withdraw from the International Criminal Court, calling its record selective, and urged other African states to follow.
story.display_body: Chad announced it will withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), the Hague-based tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and crimes against humanity, and called on other African Union members to follow. Chad's foreign ministry said the court's record shows "undeniable and egregious selectivity," noting that nine of the ICC's 13 investigations since 2002 have concerned African states and that only one of seven people detained came from outside Africa; the ministry framed the exit as confidence in national and African justice, not an abandonment of victims. That selectivity charge is Chad's own characterisation - the ICC counters that several of its African cases were opened at the request of the states themselves - and it lands as Chad's military leader faces opposition accusations of repression.
story.why: An African state quitting the ICC and lobbying the AU to do the same feeds a long-running push to weaken the court's reach on the continent, at a moment when its authority is already contested.

story.headline: US court rejects Credit Suisse AT1 suit
story.summary: A US appeals court upheld dismissal of an investor suit against Switzerland over the CS AT1 bond write-down, citing state immunity.
story.display_body: A US appeals court has rejected an investor lawsuit against Switzerland over the wipeout of Credit Suisse's AT1 bonds, the federal finance department (EFD) confirmed on Tuesday 28 July. The judges upheld a lower court's finding that when Switzerland's regulator wrote the bonds to zero it acted as a supervisory authority, not a market participant, and so enjoys state immunity and falls outside US jurisdiction. AT1 bonds ("additional tier 1" - subordinated debt created after the 2008 crisis that is designed to absorb losses and prop up a failing bank) worth about US$17.3 billion were written off when the Swiss state orchestrated UBS's emergency takeover of Credit Suisse in spring 2023. A group of international investors had sued in June 2024 for roughly US$370 million; they can still seek review by the full appeals court or the US Supreme Court, though the EFD says the bar for that is "very high." Separate cases continue elsewhere: Switzerland's own Federal Administrative Court partly overturned the write-down in October 2025 after complaints from some 3,600 investors - a ruling FINMA and UBS have appealed to the Federal Supreme Court - and a group of Japanese investors filed an arbitration claim at the ICSID (a World Bank body that settles investment disputes) in late 2025.
story.why: The US ruling closes one front in the global legal fight over the most contested piece of the CS rescue, but the decisive battles over whether the write-down stands are still open in Swiss courts and international arbitration.

story.headline: New heatwave grips parched Switzerland
story.summary: A fresh heatwave with peaks of 34-39C is forecast for Switzerland from midweek as drought keeps fire and fireworks bans in place before 1 August.
story.display_body: A fresh heatwave is rolling into an already parched Switzerland, with SRF Meteo forecasting temperatures of 34-39C at their peak on Thursday 30 July and the hot spell likely to last into the first week of August. The 30C mark was expected to be passed again in the north on Tuesday, widespread 35C from Wednesday 29 July, with the highest readings in northwest Switzerland, the lower Aare valley and around Geneva, plus several "tropical nights" (when temperatures stay above 20C) in cities and by the larger lakes. Forecasters see no substantial cooling or the sustained, widespread rain needed to break the drought before mid-August; open-fire and fireworks bans remain in force across much of the country ahead of the 1 August national holiday (this Saturday), and a field fire near Koblenz (Aargau) spread into woodland on Tuesday.
story.why: This is the same heat-and-drought spell fuelling the wildfires in France and Spain now reaching Swiss soil, and it means the country's biggest civic holiday will again be marked under near-total fire restrictions.

story.headline: Opus 5 tops the ARC-AGI leaderboard
story.summary: Claude Opus 5 at max reasoning posts record ARC-AGI scores on ARC Prize's official scorecard.
story.display_body: On ARC Prize's official scorecard, Claude Opus 5 at maximum reasoning effort scores 97.5% on ARC-AGI-1 and 90.4% on ARC-AGI-2, and is the top model on the newer interactive ARC-AGI-3 at 30.2%. ARC-AGI is a suite of abstract visual-reasoning puzzles deliberately built to resist memorization — you infer a hidden rule from a few examples and apply it — and ARC-AGI-2 in particular was designed to stay hard for frontier LLMs, which makes a 90% figure a notable jump rather than a routine leaderboard nudge.
story.why: ARC-AGI is the benchmark most explicitly aimed at fluid reasoning rather than recalled knowledge, so a frontier model clearing 90% on its second-generation set is a real signal about where reasoning models are — while ARC-AGI-3, still at 30%, marks how far the interactive, multi-step version remains from solved. These are ARC Prize's verified scores on its semi-private set, not a vendor's self-report, which is what makes them worth citing.

story.headline: DeepSeek's MLA splits content from position
story.summary: A mechanistic study of Multi-head Latent Attention finds its low-rank cache keeps content and discards position.
story.display_body: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) — the attention variant introduced in DeepSeek-V2 that squeezes the key-value cache through a shared low-rank bottleneck (a compression step that cuts memory ~81% at inference, the main cost of long context) — is now in production models, but nobody had checked what the bottleneck keeps and what it throws away. Training a small 114M-parameter transformer end to end and probing its internals, the authors find the compressed channel learns an almost pure content representation: it retains entity identity (98%) while discarding positional information, which the model reconstructs elsewhere.
story.why: MLA is one of the load-bearing tricks behind cheap long context, copied into models most people now use, yet it was adopted for its memory savings without anyone knowing what it costs representationally. A clean it separates content from position, and here's where position goes is exactly the kind of grounding that lets the next architecture tweak be deliberate rather than superstitious. That the study runs at 114M rather than frontier scale is the honest caveat.

story.headline: Bounding the train-inference gap stabilizes RL
story.summary: ACRL adaptively bounds the discrepancy between training and inference engines to stabilize LLM reinforcement learning.
story.display_body: When labs fine-tune a model with reinforcement learning (RL — training by reward signal rather than by copying examples), the code that generates candidate answers and the code that updates the weights are usually separate engines, and the generator often runs in lower-precision arithmetic to go fast. That mismatch makes the two disagree about what the model actually said, and past a point the training destabilizes. ACRL (Adaptive Control RL) measures the discrepancy live and keeps it inside a safe band; as a side effect it raises policy entropy, nudging the model to keep exploring rather than collapsing onto one answer.
story.why: RL post-training is now how reasoning models are made, and our run diverged and we don't know why is a common and expensive failure. Naming the training-inference gap as a controllable quantity — not an unavoidable artifact of the systems stack — turns a mysterious instability into a dial.

story.headline: What reward models actually memorize
story.summary: A study finds reward models lean on length and compliance and memorize dataset-specific shortcuts, not answer quality.
story.display_body: A reward model is the learned judge that scores answers during alignment training — get it wrong and every model trained against it inherits the bias. Measuring counterfactual memorization (how much a specific training pair changed the model versus what it generalized), the authors show reward models misallocate memory to easy, high-margin preference pairs, latch onto dataset-specific shortcuts like which model produced an answer, and over-generalize crude correlates of human preference — longer answers, more compliant tone — when they meet unfamiliar comparisons.
story.why: the model is well-aligned ultimately rests on the reward model judging quality rather than surface features, and this is direct evidence that today's discriminatively-trained judges are not yet doing that in context-dependent cases. It's a caution for anyone treating a reward score as ground truth.

story.headline: RLVR extended to open-ended tasks
story.summary: RLSVR transforms open-ended tasks into self-verifiable proxy environments to extend verifiable-reward RL beyond math and code.
story.display_body: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) drove much of the recent reasoning-model progress, but it only works where correctness can be checked automatically — arithmetic, unit tests — leaving open-ended writing or dialogue dependent on costly, biased LLM-judges. RLSVR (the S for self-verifiable) borrows a trick from self-supervised learning: it transforms an open-ended task into a proxy task the model can grade itself against (for example, reconstructing a corrupted target), manufacturing a verifiable reward from the data rather than an external judge.
story.why: the biggest limitation on the RLVR recipe is the shrinking supply of tasks with a clean automatic grader. If self-verifiable proxies hold up, that unlocks the same training machinery for the messy majority of tasks where is this good? has no unit test — though whether the proxy actually rewards the quality you care about is the thing to scrutinize.

story.headline: CoT-faithfulness detectors fail where models err
story.summary: Auditing chain-of-thought unfaithfulness detection finds no signal beats chance where models answer incorrectly.
story.display_body: A chain-of-thought (CoT) — the written reasoning a model shows before its answer — only supports oversight if it is faithful, i.e. the stated steps actually produced the answer rather than being a plausible after-the-fact story. Auditing black-box detectors of unfaithful CoT against human-annotated data, the authors find answer correctness structures everything: 69% of annotated unfaithfulness happens on wrong answers, and on those wrong answers no tested detector beats chance. Just knowing the answer is wrong (not a deployable signal) outpredicts every purpose-built detector.
story.why: a lot of safety hope rests on reading a model's reasoning to catch when it's being deceptive or shortcutting. This says the reasoning trace is least trustworthy exactly when the model is wrong — the case you most need to catch — which connects to the government-lab finding this week that evaluation-gaming often leaves no trace in the chain-of-thought at all.

story.headline: Consensus decoding blocks fine-tuning backdoors
story.summary: Aggregating next-token distributions across models trained on different sources blocks hidden misbehavior from poisoned fine-tuning.
story.display_body: Recent work shows a tiny amount of poisoned fine-tuning data can install targeted misbehavior, and even innocuous-looking data can transmit hidden preferences. Standard defenses (filtering, mixing in clean data, regularization) dampen but don't remove the effect. This paper pursues robustness through redundancy: fine-tune a separate model on each data source, then at generation time combine their next-token predictions with a consensus rule (e.g. a token-wise minimum), so anything only one poisoned source wanted gets suppressed.
story.why: as organizations fine-tune on data scraped or bought from many sources, one bad supplier can backdoor your model is a real supply-chain risk. Consensus-at-decoding is an appealingly simple mitigation — it needs no trust in any single source — at the cost of running several models.

story.headline: Data-free 4-bit attention quantization
story.summary: MXAttention quantizes attention to MXFP4 without calibration data, targeting diffusion video inference.
story.display_body: The quadratic cost of attention dominates diffusion-based video generation. MXFP4 — a 4-bit floating-point format with a small shared scale per block — promises cheap attention but usually wrecks output quality, because power-of-two scaling clips or underflows values and the softmax normalization introduces rounding error. MXAttention is a post-training method (no retraining, no calibration set) that derives an optimal scaling boundary analytically and quantizes the un-normalized softmax terms before summing them, sidestepping both problems.
story.why: 4-bit attention is one of the few remaining levers for making video generation affordable to serve, and data-free matters because gathering representative calibration data is itself a chore. A method that just works from the model's own numerics lowers the barrier — the open question, as always with aggressive quantization, is whether the quality holds up on content outside the tested set.

story.headline: KV-cache eviction as an estimation problem
story.summary: Recasts KV-cache eviction as fixed-lag smoothing, waiting a few steps before committing which tokens to keep.
story.display_body: A model serving long context has a bounded working memory (the KV-cache — the stored keys and values it attends back over) and must keep deciding which items to drop. Every deployed method — StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV — commits the instant an item arrives, guessing whether it'll be reused. This paper recasts the decision as estimating a hidden signal (will this be needed?) and points out the missing middle: fixed-lag smoothing, which waits a bounded number of steps, watches which items a correct near-future prediction actually attended to, and only then commits.
story.why: the KV-cache is the memory wall of long-context serving, and eviction policies are usually hand-designed heuristics. Casting the whole family as points on one axis — how long you wait before committing — is a genuinely clarifying frame, and it suggests a cheap way to approach the unbeatable offline optimum by measuring rather than guessing.

fields.display_body: A model serving long context has a bounded working memory (the KV-cache — the stored keys and values it attends back over) and must keep deciding which items to drop. Every deployed method — StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV — commits the instant an item arrives, guessing whether it'll be reused. This paper recasts the decision as estimating a hidden signal (will this be needed?) and points out the missing middle: fixed-lag smoothing, which waits a bounded number of steps, watches which items a correct near-future prediction actually attended to, and only then commits.
fields.why: the KV-cache is the memory wall of long-context serving, and eviction policies are usually hand-designed heuristics. Casting the whole family as points on one axis — how long you wait before committing — is a genuinely clarifying frame, and it suggests a cheap way to approach the unbeatable offline optimum by measuring rather than guessing.

story.headline: A task's minimum model capacity, read off the data
story.summary: The Entropic Bound derives a task's minimum required transformer rank and shows it is recoverable before training.
story.display_body: Scaling laws tell you how loss falls as you add parameters and compute, but not the prior question: for a fixed task, what is the least capacity that can solve it? Working in a simplified linear-attention model, the paper proves that the intrinsic rank of the token-mixing operation is a tight lower bound — any model below it pays an unavoidable error penalty — that gradient descent recovers this rank, and that the rank can be estimated from the data before you train.
story.why: most capacity decisions are made by trial, expense, and folklore. A principled this task needs at least rank r*, computable up front is the kind of theory that, if it transfers from the linear surrogate to real attention (the paper's honest open problem), could tell you how big a model has to be before you spend the GPU-hours.

story.headline: A German-first 2.7B model for phones
story.summary: ELMOD is a compact German language model trained on 55k H100 hours for on-device inference.
story.display_body: ELMOD is a compact (2.7-billion-parameter) German language model trained on 55,000 H100-GPU-hours using only publicly available data, aimed at running on resource-constrained hardware. Its contribution is less the size than the recipe: German-specific data preprocessing that handles the language's heavy compounding, rich morphology, and orthographic quirks — pipelines tuned for English handle these badly — plus quality filtering and rephrasing.
story.why: most small on-device models are English-first, and European-language users get the leftovers. A documented, publicly-trained German model is a small but concrete data point for non-English on-device inference — relevant in a market (Switzerland included) where the working languages aren't the ones the big labs optimize for.

story.headline: Kimi K3 open weights go live
story.summary: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3's weights on schedule, a multimodal open-weight MoE with ~2.78T total parameters.
story.display_body: Moonshot AI released the weights for Kimi K3, the multimodal open-weight mixture-of-experts (MoE — a model where only a small subset of expert sub-networks fires per token, so a huge total parameter count stays cheap to run) it had announced earlier in July with a scheduled 27 July drop. The Hugging Face model card now shows the model live — roughly 2.78-trillion total parameters, image-and-text input, an other open-weight license — and it has already passed ~99,000 downloads and 7,300 likes, with hosted inference offered through Together, Fireworks and Featherless.
story.why: the announcement was covered when it landed; what's new is that the weights actually shipped on schedule, putting a near-frontier ~3-trillion-parameter open model into anyone's hands — the practical event behind the abstract China's open models are near parity story, and the concrete thing the week's US policy debate is reacting to.

story.headline: Microsoft ships MAI-Cyber-1-Flash
story.summary: Microsoft launched a compact cybersecurity model scoring 96% on CyberGym inside its MDASH agent system, escalating hard cases to OpenAI.
story.display_body: Microsoft unveiled MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, a small security model (from its MAI-Thinking-1 line) embedded in its MDASH multi-agent system, plus Perception, an agent that monitors and mitigates threats in real time. The combination scores 96% on CyberGym — a benchmark measuring how well a model finds real security flaws in large codebases — which Microsoft says is 12 points above the Mythos system and ahead of Gemini and GPT; it claims ~50% lower cost because the small model handles 90% of tasks and escalates only the hardest to GPT-5.4.
story.why: the framing is telling — Microsoft positioning itself as an orchestrator routing most work to a cheap in-house model and buying frontier reasoning only when needed is the cheap specialized model below, expensive frontier above pattern showing up across the industry, and a shift for a company whose cloud growth ran on exclusive OpenAI distribution. Every number here is Microsoft's own on a benchmark it selected; independent evaluation is the thing to wait for.

story.headline: Delhi court denies ANI injunction on OpenAI
story.summary: The Delhi High Court denied Indian agency ANI a preliminary injunction against OpenAI, turning on training-data dates and RAG.
story.display_body: In an interim ruling, Judge Amit Bansal rejected news agency Asian News International's bid to block OpenAI over copyrighted material used in training and reproduced in ChatGPT outputs. A decisive factual point: OpenAI showed GPT-4 and GPT-4o were trained on data through April 2022 and April 2024, while the ANI articles cited were mostly from August-September 2024 — so they couldn't have been in the training set. The court's preliminary view was that any similarity came from retrieval-augmented generation (RAG — the model fetching live web content at answer time, like a search engine) rather than memorized training data; ANI hadn't addressed RAG, and even with adversarial prompts explicitly demanding exact reproduction it produced no verbatim copy. The judge noted that RAG outputs could count as communication to the public, a question left for the main proceedings.
story.why: this is an early, reasoned decision separating three distinct questions courts keep conflating — memorization of training data, real-time RAG retrieval, and the copyrightability of facts and headlines — and it turned on datable evidence rather than vibes. It's an interim win for OpenAI, not a final ruling, and the RAG communication to the public question it flagged is the one with the longest reach for how retrieval-based AI is regulated.

story.headline: US weighs targeted bans on Chinese open models
story.summary: NYT reports the White House favors model-specific bans over a blanket ban on Chinese open-weight models.
story.display_body: The New York Times reports that the Trump administration, preparing to tighten rules on Chinese open-weight models, favors targeted bans on specific models over a wholesale block, citing national-security concerns; the Times also reports Anthropic and OpenAI are privately lobbying to restrict Chinese open models — even as OpenAI publicly signed, alongside Google DeepMind, an open letter opposing regulation of open-weight AI. The reporting notes that on cybersecurity benchmarks even recent releases such as Kimi K3 still trail leading Western models.
story.why: the same firms are on both sides of the open-weights fight — publicly against regulation, privately lobbying to curb the Chinese models that undercut them on price. That contradiction is the story: read the national-security framing alongside the plain commercial pressure from cheap Chinese open weights, and note this is reported policy deliberation, not enacted rule.
